title: Chapter 28 — Ahab
paragraphs: For several days after leaving Nantucket, nothing was seen of Captain Ahab above the hatches. The mates regularly relieved each other at the watches, and for all that could be seen to the contrary, they seemed to be the only commanders of the ship; only, they sometimes came out of the cabin with orders so sudden and peremptory that it was plain, after all, that they were only commanding on someone else's behalf. Yes, their supreme lord and dictator was there, though so far unseen by any eyes not permitted to penetrate the now sacred retreat of the cabin.

Every time I came up on deck from my watches below, I instantly looked aft to see if any strange face was visible; for my first vague uneasiness about the unknown captain, now in the seclusion of the sea, had become almost an agitation. This was strangely heightened at times by the ragged Elijah's diabolical, incoherent ramblings, which came back to me uninvited, with a subtle energy I could not have imagined before. I could only poorly withstand them, much as in other moods I was almost ready to smile at the solemn whims of that outlandish prophet of the wharves. But whatever apprehension or uneasiness — to call it that — I felt, whenever I came to look around me in the ship, it seemed against all reason to cherish such feelings. For though the harpooners, with the great body of the crew, were a far more barbaric, heathenish, and motley set than any of the tame merchant-ship companies I had known before, I still put this down — and rightly — to the fierce uniqueness of the very nature of that wild Scandinavian calling in which I had so recklessly embarked. But it was above all the look of the three chief officers of the ship, the mates, that was most strongly fitted to allay these colorless misgivings and to inspire confidence and cheerfulness about every prospect of the voyage. Three better, more promising sea-officers and men, each in his own different way, could not easily be found, and every one of them was American: a Nantucketer, a Vineyarder, a Cape man. Now, since it was Christmas when the ship shot out of her harbor, for a while we had biting polar weather, though all the time we were running away from it to the southward; and with every degree and minute of latitude we sailed, we gradually left that merciless winter and all its intolerable weather behind us. It was on one of those mornings of the transition, less threatening but still gray and gloomy enough, when with a fair wind the ship was rushing through the water with a vengeful sort of leaping and melancholy speed, that I climbed to the deck at the call of the forenoon watch; and the moment I leveled my gaze toward the taffrail at the stern, foreboding shivers ran over me. Reality outran apprehension: Captain Ahab stood upon his quarter-deck.

There seemed to be no sign of ordinary bodily illness about him, nor of recovery from any. He looked like a man cut down from the stake when the fire has swept over and withered all the limbs without consuming them, or taking away one particle of their compact, aged robustness. His whole tall, broad form seemed made of solid bronze, and shaped in an unalterable mold, like Cellini's cast Perseus. Threading its way out from among his gray hairs, and continuing right down one side of his tawny, scorched face and neck until it disappeared into his clothing, you saw a slender, rod-like mark, livid and whitish. It resembled that vertical seam sometimes made in the straight, lofty trunk of a great tree when the lightning from above darts tearing down it, and, without wrenching off a single twig, peels and grooves out the bark from top to bottom before running off into the soil, leaving the tree still green and alive, but branded. Whether that mark was born with him, or whether it was the scar left by some desperate wound, no one could say for certain. By some unspoken agreement, little or no mention was made of it throughout the voyage, especially by the mates. But once Tashtego's senior, an old Gay Head Indian among the crew, superstitiously asserted that Ahab was not branded that way until he was a full forty years old, and that it came upon him not in the fury of any mortal fight, but in an elemental struggle at sea. Yet this wild hint seemed, by inference, to be contradicted by what a gray Manxman hinted — an old, sepulchral man who, having never sailed out of Nantucket before, had never until now laid eyes on wild Ahab. Nevertheless, the old sea traditions, the immemorial credulities, popularly credited this old Manxman with preternatural powers of discernment. So no white sailor seriously contradicted him when he said that if Captain Ahab should ever be laid out peacefully — which might hardly come to pass, so he muttered — then whoever performed that last office for the dead would find a birthmark on him from crown to sole.

So powerfully did the whole grim aspect of Ahab affect me, and the livid brand which streaked it, that for the first few moments I hardly noticed that not a little of this overpowering grimness was owing to the barbaric white leg on which he partly stood. I had heard earlier that this ivory leg had been fashioned at sea from the polished bone of the sperm whale's jaw. "Aye, he was dismasted off Japan," the old Gay Head Indian once said, "but like his dismasted ship, he shipped another mast without coming home for it. He has a quiver of them."

I was struck by the singular posture he maintained. On each side of the Pequod's quarter-deck, and pretty close to the mizzen shrouds, an auger hole had been bored about half an inch or so into the plank. His bone leg was steadied in that hole. One arm raised, holding onto a shroud, Captain Ahab stood erect, staring straight out beyond the ship's ever-pitching bow. There was an infinity of the firmest fortitude, a determined, unsurrendering willfulness, in the fixed and fearless, forward dedication of that gaze. He spoke not a word, nor did his officers say anything to him. Yet by their every small gesture and expression, they clearly showed the uneasy, if not painful, awareness of being under a troubled master's eye. And more than that — moody, stricken Ahab stood before them with a crucifixion in his face, with all the nameless, regal, overpowering dignity of some mighty grief.

Soon after his first appearance on deck, he withdrew to his cabin. But after that morning, he was visible to the crew every day — either standing in his pivot-hole, or sitting on an ivory stool he had, or walking heavily across the deck. As the sky grew less gloomy and even began to turn a little mild, he became less and less of a recluse, as if, when the ship first sailed from home, nothing but the dead winter bleakness of the sea had kept him shut away. Gradually, he was almost constantly in the open air. But for all he said or visibly did on the deck, sunny at last, he seemed as unnecessary there as an extra mast. The Pequod was only making a passage, not actively cruising. The mates were fully capable of handling nearly all the whaling preparations that needed overseeing. So there was little or nothing outside of himself to occupy or excite Ahab now, and so to chase away, for that one interval, the clouds that were piled layer upon layer on his brow — just as all clouds always choose the loftiest peaks to pile themselves upon.

Nevertheless, before long, the warm, warbling persuasiveness of the pleasant holiday weather we came into seemed gradually to charm him out of his mood. For as when the red-cheeked dancing girls, April and May, come tripping home to the wintry, misanthropic woods, even the barest, most rugged, most thunder-split old oak will at least send out a few green sprouts to welcome such glad-hearted visitors, so Ahab did, in the end, respond a little to the playful enticements of that girlish air. More than once he put forth the faint blossom of a look which, in any other man, would soon have flowered into a smile.
